/recaps/1/pages/0/segments/0/text: María rose from a cloth merchant’s daughter to become the Marquesa de Montemayor. She resisted marriage, yet eventually entered the chapel amid the guests’ derision. Her daughter’s birth gave her one child on whom to lavish all the love she had never received. Clara grew up under that anxious attention, needing ever more distance. The more her mother feared rejection, the harder she tried to please and the more she talked. When Clara shut the door, María waited outside for an answer that would reassure her. She remembered the fears of her own childhood; that memory alone could not keep her from becoming a burden to another child.
/recaps/1/pages/1/title: A letter cannot shorten the sea
/recaps/1/pages/1/segments/0/text: Clara chose a marriage that would take her to Spain. She boarded calmly, leaving her mother on the shore. Four years later, María was at last allowed to visit. Both resolved to change, and both wounded the other again. Before dawn María kissed her daughter’s door and returned to Peru. She entrusted to letters the feelings they could scarcely bear face to face. She collected jokes, read books and polished her sentences, hoping Clara would linger over them. Those letters survived, chiefly because her son-in-law preserved them. Their writer still wanted only a little closeness. Alone on her balcony, she also recognized the wish to control within her longing for an answer, but could not let it go.
/recaps/1/pages/2/title: The child entrusted with a future
/recaps/1/pages/2/segments/0/text: Fearing that no one would continue her work, the abbess chose Pepita beside the laundry trough. She gave the girl difficult errands, taught her about wards and accounts, then sent her to the Marquesa’s house to learn about life beyond the convent. Pepita was proud to be trusted and afraid she was unequal to it. In her new home, bullying servants and the lady’s wavering affection left her no one she could safely confide in. Once the Marquesa told her to wait outside a church, then left by another door. Even after learning that she had gone, Pepita returned to the street corner to wait. She knew how to hold fast to a duty; she did not yet know how to ask for help with her own troubles.
/recaps/1/pages/3/segments/0/text: At the theatre, Camila improvised a song mocking the Marquesa and won the audience’s applause. Pepita understood and led her mistress out. The Marquesa, absorbed in thoughts of her distant daughter, had scarcely heard. Sent by the Viceroy to apologize, the actress mistook her bewilderment for forgiveness and felt real shame. María described a tender reconciliation with Clara. It was only a dream she had had many times. When news of Clara’s pregnancy arrived, her mother sought help in prohibitions, charms and prayers, then took Pepita on a mountain pilgrimage. While her mistress hurried to the shrine, the girl stayed at the inn to arrange trunks, charcoal and food, making an unfamiliar room a place they could inhabit.
/recaps/1/pages/4/title: What survived, what was torn up
/recaps/1/pages/4/segments/0/text: The clear mountain air briefly quieted María. Clara’s new letter still hurt, but she no longer rushed to seek a guarantee. Alone, Pepita wrote to ask for a few days back at the convent and a few words from the abbess. While the girl was downstairs, the Marquesa read her appeal. Before supper Pepita refused to send it, calling it insufficiently brave; later she tore it up. Her words made María reconsider her own demands. She wrote anew the letter later known as Letter LVI, calling it her first. As dawn approached she looked in on the sleeping girl. They set out for Lima two days later. The appeal for help did not survive; the mother’s new letter reached people who would live on.
/recaps/2/pages/0/title: Two people who need no explanation
/recaps/2/pages/0/segments/0/text: Manuel and Esteban were found in a basket outside the convent and grew up under the abbess’s care. They heard many stories. As a boy, Manuel insisted that if the brothers had been present at the Crucifixion, they would have stopped it. Grown up, they copied texts, loaded cargo and took temporary jobs. Strangers’ jokes about their identical faces made them avoid appearing together in the street. They also had a private language invented in childhood. When the Archbishop wanted to record its words, that intimacy made them too embarrassed to speak. To others they seemed uncommunicative. Together they needed few words to know that someone was there.
/recaps/2/pages/1/segments/0/text: One evening of free admission, Esteban left the theatre first; Manuel stayed to watch Camila dance. His attraction deepened. He agreed to write her secret love letters, telling even his brother nothing. Their declarations and anger were addressed to other men. One late night she came to their rented room to dictate. From his bed, Esteban mistook their close whispering for an intimacy he could not share. Seeing his brother’s pain, Manuel announced that he would stop writing for her. Esteban said there was no need to change on his account and even tried to leave in the rain. Both stayed. They did not return to the quarrel. Silence was restored, but the distance between them had not been fully explained.
/recaps/2/pages/2/title: A wet cloth and one name
/recaps/2/pages/2/segments/0/text: Manuel injured his knee and grew steadily worse. The doctor ordered cold applications every hour. Esteban stayed to replace the wet cloths, only to find that these were his brother’s moments of greatest pain. Curses poured out in his illness and were retracted when he was lucid. Both kinds of words truly wounded the caregiver; they cannot simply be assembled into a final confession. Manuel died on the third night. The abbess came to arrange the burial. The survivor would not enter the building and even gave his dead brother’s name when asked who he was. As the funeral moved through the city, he followed along parallel streets, seeing it from a distance and losing it from a distance.
/recaps/2/pages/3/segments/0/text: Esteban wandered for a long time, sometimes working, sometimes suddenly leaving. He went to Camila’s dressing room but could not speak. Outside the convent, the abbess twice called him her friend; he turned and ran. At last she thought of the Captain and asked him to find the young man in Cuzco. The Captain offered work and an invitation to supper. Here Esteban spoke his own name again. Over the meal he asked for constant work aboard ship and for no one to be told his history. The conversation did not lift his grief, but it left another meeting and a journey together still to come.
/recaps/2/pages/4/title: They were meant to meet again
/recaps/2/pages/4/segments/0/text: Esteban wanted an advance on his wages to give the abbess a present from himself and his dead brother. What to buy had not yet been decided. The Captain agreed, recognizing in the young man his own grief for his daughter. The next day Esteban withdrew his promise and returned upstairs in crisis. The Captain entered and kept him among the living, without promising that a few words could make grief disappear. Later they set out together and separated at the bridge: the Captain went down into the gorge to supervise the cargo, while Esteban took the footbridge. They were meant to meet again. The bridge broke. Setting out had been an attempt to continue living; it brought no guarantee from fate.
/recaps/3/pages/0/segments/0/text: Pio left home in childhood and made a living by his memory, connections and ingenuity. He loved freedom, beautiful women and Spanish literature. He knew many people’s secrets, yet often had only trained dogs and birds for company at home. He noticed twelve-year-old Camila singing in a café and paid to take her away. First came hot soup, a small bed and an end to beatings; strict training followed. They toured together with their clothes in one shawl, enduring poverty and danger. He watched her talent grow rapidly, while she found work she wanted to give herself to. Their closeness always coexisted with unequal power.
/recaps/3/pages/1/segments/0/text: Even after the audience was satisfied, Camila had to face Pio’s whistling and criticism. The dressing room held tears and rehearsals that lasted until dawn. He could help her understand a detail, yet often drove her by withholding praise. On the night they performed for the poet’s granddaughter, they also shared a true artistic joy. Later, the Viceroy’s suppers brought manners, experience and status. Pio was pleased to see these improve her acting. Camila still had to bear the weariness of love, daily life and her body. The life she wanted was not solely in the service of the next speech.
/recaps/3/pages/2/segments/0/text: Camila left the stage and spent years seeking respectability, making a new position for herself and her children. Walking through her mountain garden, she still waited for happiness to begin. Her frail son Jaime was glad simply to be in the sunshine. Pio visited monthly; after a cold reception he went upstairs to the children, still hoping their former closeness might return. In their dusk conversation in the garden, he belatedly admitted how little praise he had given her. He proposed Madrid or an island of his dreams. Camila refused to return to the theatre, then apologized after mentioning the child’s attack that afternoon. Finally she kissed his fingers. The gesture brought warmth without making their futures one again.
/recaps/3/pages/3/segments/0/text: After smallpox, Camila returned gifts, moved to her villa and refused visitors. She understood their concern as pity tinged with superiority, gradually shutting out help as well. Pio cared for the children and managed the estate. At last allowed inside, he unexpectedly opened a door she believed locked. The mirror showed her secret attempt to powder her face, and the visitor’s surprise. Furious, she drove him out and forbade him even the courtyard. Back in Lima he could not rest. He climbed the road again, imagining that he might educate Jaime. His good intentions and his intrusions coexist; neither cancels the other.
/recaps/3/pages/4/segments/0/text: Pio imitated a weeping girl to draw Camila outside, then asked to take Jaime to the city for a year’s education. Refused, he pressed her by demanding repayment of a debt, then withdrew the demand for money. Camila finally set a condition: first ask whether the child wished to go. Jaime appeared next day with a gold coin from his mother and a little stone to look at when sleepless. The jolting journey made him ill, so Pio carried him on his shoulder. Before the bridge they met the Captain and spoke to María and Pepita. Their plan to rest on the other side was never fulfilled. Education, homecoming and voyage all remained unfinished. Those who survived still had to live with love, wrongs and care.
/timelines/2/rows/4: The wound and the wet cloth
